items.title: 61426_Jacques Butler oral history interview
items.q: The interviewee discusses Johnny Hodges in the context of the Ellington Band's radio broadcasts and public perception, stating 'the only way they could hear them was on the radio' and referring to the band members collectively ('them'), without indicating a personal interaction or direct professiona

ctx.x: You know, Rex Stewart had in his book, Jazz Masters of the 1930's that initially because the guys of the Ellington Band were playing the Cotton Club and people didn't like the Cotton Club because of its racial policies, he said at first the guys tried to kind of write the band off, you know, they just kind of didn't pay much attention to him. But then big guys like Johnny Hodges and Barney Bigard and others started coming around to the Rhythm Club and other places and started jamming, you know.

Yeah, because the only way they could hear them was on the radio. And when they started hearing them on that radio, they understood. They had to understand, man. They had to understand. This was them. And on the radio every night from the Cotton Club and therefore -- there wasn't no band could touch them. Fletcher was downtown. Fletcher was downtown playing these waltzes and everything else. So the only time you could hear them in person was at the Savoy Ballroom when they had that battle. That's the only time…
